note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: The SI unit of electric current is the
items.explanation: One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second.

options.why: The volt is the unit of potential difference.
The ohm is the unit of resistance.
The coulomb is the unit of charge, not of current.

items.stem: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is proportional to the
items.explanation: At constant temperature the current is directly proportional to the potential difference across the conductor.

options.why: Current is inversely proportional to resistance, not directly.
Length affects resistance, and current falls as length rises.
The relation is linear, not quadratic.

items.stem: The SI unit of electrical resistance is the
items.explanation: One ohm is the resistance of a conductor through which one ampere flows for one volt applied.

options.why: The ampere is the unit of current.
The volt is the unit of potential difference.
The watt is the unit of power.

items.stem: An ammeter is always connected in
items.explanation: An ammeter measures the current through a component, so it must carry that current and is connected in series.

options.why: A voltmeter is connected in parallel; an ammeter in parallel would short the circuit.
Only series is correct for an ammeter.
It must be part of the circuit whose current it measures.

items.stem: Three resistors of 2, 3 and 5 ohms are joined in series. The total resistance is
items.explanation: In series the resistances simply add, so the total is 2 plus 3 plus 5.

options.why: That is the parallel combination, not the series one.
Resistances add rather than multiply in series.
That would be the average, which has no physical meaning here.

items.stem: The resistance of a wire increases when its
items.explanation: Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area of cross-section.

options.why: A thicker wire has lower resistance, not higher.
For a metal, lowering the temperature lowers the resistance.
Resistance is a property of the wire, not of the current.

items.stem: A bulb rated 60 W works on 240 V. The current through it is
items.explanation: Current is power divided by voltage, that is 60 divided by 240.

options.why: This divides voltage by power, inverting the relation.
This multiplies power by voltage instead of dividing.
This subtracts rather than divides.

items.stem: Adding another resistor in parallel to an existing combination always
items.explanation: A parallel path gives the current an extra route, so the total resistance falls below the smallest branch.

options.why: Adding a path cannot make it harder for current to flow.
An additional route always lowers the total.

options.text: makes the total equal to the new resistor
options.why: The total is always less than the smallest individual branch.

items.stem: According to Joule's law, the heat produced in a resistor is proportional to
items.explanation: Heat equals I squared times R times t, so it varies as the square of the current.

options.why: Doubling the current quadruples the heat, so the relation is quadratic.
More current produces more heat, not less.

options.text: the square root of the current
options.why: The dependence is on the square, not the square root.

items.stem: A fuse wire is made of a material with a low melting point and
items.explanation: A high resistance makes it heat up quickly, so it melts and breaks the circuit before the wiring is damaged.

options.why: A very low resistance would not heat enough to melt.
A high melting point would prevent it acting at all.
With no resistance no heat would be produced.

items.stem: Define electric current.
items.answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb per second, so I equals Q divided by t.

items.stem: Define potential difference and state its unit.
items.answer: Potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other. Its unit is the volt, and one volt is one joule per coulomb.

items.stem: Why does no current flow in an open circuit?
items.answer: Current needs a continuous conducting path from one terminal of the cell to the other. An open circuit has a break in that path, so the charge has nowhere to flow and the current is zero.

items.stem: What is resistivity, and how does it differ from resistance?
items.answer: Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section, and its unit is the ohm metre. It is a property of the material alone, whereas resistance also depends on the length and thickness of the particular piece.

items.stem: Write three expressions for electric power.
items.answer: P equals V times I, P equals I squared times R, and P equals V squared divided by R. All three are equivalent, and which one is convenient depends on the quantities known.

items.stem: What is one kilowatt hour in joules?
items.answer: One kilowatt hour is 1000 watts acting for 3600 seconds, so it is 1000 times 3600, which is 3.6 times 10 to the power 6 joules. It is the unit in which electricity is billed and is called one unit.

items.stem: Why are domestic appliances connected in parallel rather than in series?
items.answer: In parallel each appliance receives the full supply voltage, each can be switched independently, and a fault in one does not stop the others. In series the voltage would divide among them, all would have to be on together, and one failure would break the whole circuit.

items.stem: Why is copper used for connecting wires but nichrome for a heating element?
items.answer: Copper has a very low resistivity, so long wires carry current with little wasted heat, which is what a connector should do. Nichrome has a high resistivity and does not oxidise readily even when red hot, so it produces the heat deliberately and survives repeated heating, which is what an element must do.

items.stem: State Ohm's law, write its mathematical form and state the conditions under which it holds.
items.answer: Ohm's law states that the electric current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided the temperature and the physical conditions of the conductor remain constant. In symbols, V is proportional to I, and writing the constant of proportionality as R gives V equals I times R, where R is the resistance of the conductor. A graph of V against I is therefore a straight line through the origin whose slope is the resistance. The conditions matter. The temperature must be constant, because the resistance of a metal rises as it heats, so a wire carrying a large current departs from the straight line. The law also applies to metallic conductors and not to all devices: a filament lamp, a diode or a semiconductor gives a curved graph and is described as non-ohmic. Ohm's law is therefore best regarded as a property that many conductors possess under steady conditions rather than as a universal law of nature.

items.stem: Describe the components of a simple electric circuit and the function of each.
items.answer: A cell or battery provides the potential difference that drives the charge round the circuit, converting chemical energy into electrical energy. Connecting wires, usually of copper because of its very low resistivity, provide the conducting path. A switch or plug key makes and breaks that path, so the circuit can be opened and closed at will. A resistor or an appliance is the component in which the electrical energy is converted into some other form, heat in a heater, light and heat in a lamp, or motion in a motor. An ammeter, connected in series, measures the current flowing. A voltmeter, connected in parallel across a component, measures the potential difference across it. A fuse, connected in series in the live wire, protects the circuit by melting if the current becomes dangerously large. Conventional current is taken to flow from the positive terminal of the cell round the external circuit to the negative terminal, which is opposite to the actual direction of electron flow.

items.stem: Derive the formula for resistors in series and state the properties of such a combination.
items.answer: Let three resistors R1, R2 and R3 be joined end to end and connected to a cell of potential difference V. Because there is only one path, the same current I flows through each. The potential difference divides among them, so V equals V1 plus V2 plus V3. Applying Ohm's law to each, V1 equals I R1, V2 equals I R2 and V3 equals I R3. Let the single resistance that could replace the three be Rs, so that V equals I Rs. Substituting, I Rs equals I R1 plus I R2 plus I R3, and dividing throughout by I gives Rs equals R1 plus R2 plus R3. So resistances in series simply add. The properties follow: the current is the same through every resistor, the potential differences add to the supply voltage and divide in proportion to the resistances, and the total resistance is greater than the largest individual resistance. A practical consequence is that a break anywhere stops the current everywhere, which is why series wiring is unsuitable for household circuits.

items.stem: Derive the formula for resistors in parallel and state the properties of such a combination.
items.answer: Let three resistors R1, R2 and R3 be joined between the same two points and connected to a cell of potential difference V. Because each is joined across the same two points, the potential difference across each is the same and equal to V. The current divides among the branches, so I equals I1 plus I2 plus I3. Applying Ohm's law to each branch, I1 equals V divided by R1, and similarly for the others. Let the single resistance that could replace the three be Rp, so that I equals V divided by Rp. Substituting gives V over Rp equals V over R1 plus V over R2 plus V over R3, and dividing throughout by V gives one over Rp equals one over R1 plus one over R2 plus one over R3. So the reciprocals add. The properties follow: the potential difference is the same across every branch, the currents add to the total and divide in inverse proportion to the resistances, and the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance. These are exactly the properties wanted in a house, which is why domestic appliances are wired in parallel.

items.stem: State Joule's law of heating, derive it, and give three practical applications.
items.answer: Joule's law states that the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current, to the resistance and to the time for which the current flows: H equals I squared R t. To derive it, consider a charge Q driven through a potential difference V. The work done is Q times V, and since Q equals I times t the work is V I t. If all of this work appears as heat, and V equals I R by Ohm's law, then H equals I R times I times t, that is I squared R t. Three applications follow. An electric heater, iron or toaster uses a high-resistance element of nichrome so that a large amount of heat is produced deliberately. An electric bulb uses a tungsten filament whose resistance is high and whose melting point is very high, so it becomes hot enough to glow. A fuse uses a short piece of wire of low melting point in series with the circuit, so that an excessive current heats it enough to melt it and break the circuit before the wiring is damaged. The same law explains an unwanted effect: the heat lost in long transmission cables, which is why power is transmitted at high voltage and low current.

items.stem: Explain why electrical energy is transmitted at high voltage, using the power formulae.
items.answer: The power delivered to a consumer is P equals V times I, so a given amount of power can be sent either as a large current at low voltage or a small current at high voltage. The loss in the transmission cable, however, is governed by Joule's law: the heat wasted in the cable is I squared times R times t, where R is the resistance of the cable itself. Notice that the loss depends on the square of the current and not on the voltage. So if the voltage is raised by a factor of ten, the current needed to carry the same power falls by a factor of ten, and the loss in the cable falls by a factor of one hundred. This is a very large saving, and it is why generating stations step the voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long-distance transmission and step it down again near the consumer. Two further points follow. The cable's resistance can also be reduced by making it thicker, but copper is expensive and a thick cable is heavy, so raising the voltage is the cheaper route. And high voltage brings its own problems of insulation and safety, which is why it is stepped down before entering houses. The choice is therefore a compromise, with the physics of I squared R losses driving it towards high voltage.

items.stem: Explain the four factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends, giving the relation for each.
items.answer: First, length. Resistance is directly proportional to the length of the conductor, since a longer wire offers a longer obstructed path to the moving charge. Doubling the length doubles the resistance. Second, area of cross-section. Resistance is inversely proportional to the area, since a thicker wire offers more room for the charge to pass. Doubling the area halves the resistance. Combining these two, R equals rho times L divided by A. Third, the nature of the material, expressed by the resistivity rho, which is the resistance of unit length and unit area of that material and has units of ohm metre. Metals have very low resistivity, from about 10 to the power minus 8 ohm metre for silver and copper; alloys such as nichrome and manganin are around 10 to the power minus 6; and insulators such as rubber and glass are enormously higher. Fourth, temperature. The resistance of a metal rises as it is heated, because the vibrating atoms obstruct the moving electrons more, which is why a lamp filament has a much higher resistance when lit than when cold. In semiconductors the opposite happens and resistance falls with temperature. The first three are combined in a single formula, while temperature enters as the condition under which that formula is applied, and this is why Ohm's law is stated at constant temperature.

items.stem: Explain how a fuse protects a circuit and assess why replacing it with a thicker wire is dangerous.
items.answer: A fuse is a short length of wire, made of an alloy of low melting point and comparatively high resistance, connected in series in the live wire of a circuit. Under normal conditions the current heats it only slightly and it carries the current without trouble. If a fault occurs, such as a short circuit or the overloading of a socket by too many appliances, the current rises sharply. Since the heat produced follows I squared R t, even a modest rise in current produces a large rise in heating, and the fuse wire melts. The circuit is thereby broken before the current can overheat the house wiring, set fire to insulation or destroy the appliances. The fuse is rated slightly above the normal working current of the circuit it protects. Replacing it with a thicker wire, or with any wire of higher rating, is dangerous precisely because it defeats this design. The thicker wire has lower resistance and a larger cross-section, so it needs a far greater current before it melts, and the fault current that would have blown the correct fuse now passes freely. The heating then occurs where it was never intended, in the fixed wiring inside the walls, which cannot be inspected and which has no protection of its own. The result may be melted insulation, a short circuit between live and neutral and a fire. In short, the fuse is deliberately the weakest point of the circuit, and strengthening it moves the weakest point somewhere far more expensive and far less visible.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A graph of V against I for a metal wire is a straight line. Reason (R): Ohm's law makes V proportional to I at constant temperature. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and direct proportionality is exactly what produces a straight line through the origin.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Proportionality is precisely what makes the graph straight.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Ohm's law does state that proportionality.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: A metal wire at constant temperature gives a straight line.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A voltmeter is connected in parallel. Reason (R): A voltmeter has very high resistance. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and the high resistance is what allows it to be placed in parallel without drawing appreciable current.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: High resistance is precisely what makes parallel connection harmless.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A voltmeter genuinely has very high resistance.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Measuring potential difference across a component requires parallel connection.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The total resistance of a parallel combination is less than the smallest branch. Reason (R): Each added branch provides an extra path for the current. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and an extra path can only make it easier for current to flow, so the total must fall below every branch.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The extra path is precisely why the total drops below the smallest branch.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Each parallel branch genuinely adds a route for the current.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Two 10 ohm resistors in parallel give 5 ohms, below either one.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Doubling the current doubles the heat produced. Reason (R): Heat produced is given by I squared R t. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true and is exactly what defeats the assertion: since the dependence is on the square, doubling the current quadruples the heat.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: A squared dependence means a factor of four, not two.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Joule's law genuinely gives H as I squared R t.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Doubling I multiplies I squared by four.

items.stem: State whether true or false: conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal in the external circuit.
items.explanation: This is the agreed convention, although electrons actually move the other way.

options.why: Conventional current is defined as flowing from positive to negative outside the cell.

items.stem: State whether true or false: an ammeter should have a very high resistance.
items.explanation: An ammeter is in series and must have very low resistance, or it would itself reduce the current it is measuring.

options.why: An ammeter needs very low resistance; it is the voltmeter that needs high resistance.

items.stem: State whether true or false: in a series circuit the current is the same through every component.
items.explanation: There is only one path, so the same charge passes through each component in turn.

options.why: With a single path the current has nowhere else to go, so it is identical everywhere.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the resistivity of a wire changes when the wire is stretched into a longer, thinner one.
items.explanation: Resistivity is a property of the material, so it is unchanged; the resistance rises because the length increases and the area decreases.

options.why: Stretching changes length and area and so the resistance, but not the material's resistivity.

items.stem: One volt equals one joule per ___________.
items.answer: coulomb

items.stem: The instrument used to measure current is the ___________.
items.answer: ammeter

items.stem: The commercial unit of electrical energy is the ___________.
items.answer: kilowatt hour

items.stem: Two equal resistors of R ohms in parallel give a total resistance of ___________.
items.answer: R divided by 2

items.stem: Describe the standard symbols used in circuit diagrams and explain why symbols are used rather than pictures.
items.answer: A cell is drawn as a long thin line and a short thick line side by side, the long line being the positive terminal; a battery is several such pairs in a row. A plug key or switch is shown as a break in the line with a small lever, drawn touching for a closed key and lifted for an open one. A resistor of fixed value is a plain rectangle, while a variable resistor or rheostat is a rectangle with an arrow across it. A wire is simply a line, and a junction where wires are connected is marked with a solid dot. An ammeter is a circle enclosing the letter A and a voltmeter a circle enclosing the letter V. A lamp is a circle with a cross inside. A fuse is drawn as a small rectangle or an oval with a line through it. Symbols are used rather than pictures for several reasons. They are unambiguous, since a rectangle is a resistor regardless of whether the real component is a coil, a strip or a film. They are compact, so a circuit with twenty components fits on one sheet and its structure is visible at a glance. They are international, so a diagram can be read by an engineer who shares no language with the person who drew it. And they represent only what matters electrically, leaving out the shape, size and colour of components, which is exactly the abstraction needed for analysing how the circuit behaves.

items.stem: Compare series and parallel combinations of resistors under five headings, and say which is used in houses and why.
items.answer: Current: in series the same current flows through every resistor; in parallel the current divides among the branches in inverse proportion to their resistances and the branch currents add to the total. Potential difference: in series the supply voltage divides among the resistors in proportion to their resistances; in parallel the full supply voltage appears across every branch. Total resistance: in series the resistances add, so the total exceeds the largest; in parallel the reciprocals add, so the total is less than the smallest. Independence: in series a break anywhere stops the current everywhere, and no component can be switched separately; in parallel each branch can be switched on its own and a break in one leaves the others working. Effect of adding a component: in series adding a resistor raises the total resistance and lowers the current; in parallel adding one lowers the total resistance and raises the total current drawn. Houses are wired in parallel, and every one of these headings gives a reason. Each appliance needs the full supply voltage to work at its rated power, which only parallel provides. Each must be switchable independently, since one does not want the lights to go out to switch off a fan. And a failed bulb must not disconnect everything else. The one drawback is that adding appliances raises the total current, which is why a circuit must be fused and why overloading a socket is dangerous.

items.stem: Explain the heating effect of current, why it is desirable in some devices and undesirable in others, and how each case is engineered.
items.answer: When a current flows through a resistance, the electrical energy delivered is converted into heat at a rate given by Joule's law, H equals I squared R t. The effect is unavoidable wherever there is resistance, so engineering consists in arranging for it to happen where it is wanted and not where it is not. Where the heat is wanted, the design maximises resistance at the point of use. A heater, iron, toaster or geyser uses an element of nichrome, chosen because its resistivity is high, so a short element gives a large resistance, and because it does not oxidise readily even when glowing, so it survives repeated heating. An incandescent lamp uses a tungsten filament, chosen for its high resistance and its extremely high melting point of about 3380 degrees Celsius, so it can be driven hot enough to emit light rather than merely heat; the bulb is filled with an inert gas to stop the filament oxidising. A fuse is the most direct use of all: a short wire of low melting point and high resistance is deliberately made the weakest part of the circuit so that an excessive current melts it first. Where the heat is unwanted, the design minimises both resistance and current. Connecting wires and transmission cables are made of copper or aluminium, whose resistivity is extremely low, and are made thick, since resistance falls as area rises. More importantly, power is transmitted at very high voltage, because for a given power the current is then small, and since the loss depends on the square of the current a tenfold rise in voltage cuts the cable loss a hundredfold. In a computer or a motor the heat produced is a genuine loss of efficiency and must be carried away by fins, fans or coolant, because an excessive temperature would damage the insulation. The general point is that the same equation, read in two directions, explains both the heater and the reason for the national grid.

items.stem: Explain what the rating on an electrical appliance means, and assess why an appliance may be damaged if the supply voltage differs from its rating.
items.answer: An appliance is marked with two figures, a voltage and a power, for instance 240 V and 60 W. These are not independent properties of the device; they state the power it will consume when operated at that voltage. What is actually fixed by the construction of the appliance is its resistance. From P equals V squared divided by R, the resistance of a 60 W lamp rated at 240 V is 240 squared divided by 60, which is 960 ohms, and that resistance is a property of the filament and does not change when the supply changes. Now consider operating it on a different supply. On a lower voltage, say 200 V, the power becomes 200 squared divided by 960, which is about 42 W. The lamp still works but is dimmer and runs cooler, so nothing is damaged but the appliance does not do its job; a heater on a low supply takes far longer to heat and a motor may fail to start at all, which can itself burn out the winding. On a higher voltage, say 270 V, the power becomes 270 squared divided by 960, which is about 76 W. The filament must now dissipate a quarter more heat than it was designed for, so it runs hotter than intended, evaporates faster and fails much sooner; a small excess shortens the life considerably, and a large one destroys the device at once. The assessment, then, is that the danger is asymmetric. Undervoltage generally causes poor performance and occasionally damage to motors, while overvoltage causes damage directly and quickly, because the power rises as the square of the voltage and the design has only a limited margin for the extra heat. This is why voltage stabilisers are used for sensitive equipment where the supply fluctuates, and why an appliance bought for one country's supply cannot simply be plugged into another's.

items.stem: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a resistor of 4 ohms. Find the current.
items.answer: By Ohm's law, I equals V divided by R, that is 12 divided by 4, which is 3 A. The current through the resistor is therefore 3 amperes.

items.stem: An electric heater of 1500 W is used for 3 hours daily. Find the energy used in 30 days and the cost at 6 rupees per unit.
items.answer: Power is 1500 W, that is 1.5 kW. Energy used per day is 1.5 times 3, which is 4.5 kWh. In 30 days the energy is 4.5 times 30, which is 135 kWh, that is 135 units. At 6 rupees per unit the cost is 135 times 6, which is 810 rupees. Note that the kilowatt hour is a unit of energy and not of power, since it is a power multiplied by a time.

items.stem: Resistors of 6 and 3 ohms are joined in parallel and the combination is joined in series with 4 ohms across a 12 V supply. Find the total resistance, the total current and the current in the 6 ohm resistor.
items.answer: First the parallel pair. One over Rp equals one over 6 plus one over 3, that is one over 6 plus two over 6, which is three over 6, so Rp equals 2 ohms. Note that 2 ohms is less than either branch, as it must be. Now the series total: R equals 2 plus 4, which is 6 ohms. The total current from the supply is I equals V divided by R, that is 12 divided by 6, which is 2 A. To find the branch current, first find the voltage across the parallel section: V equals I times Rp, that is 2 times 2, which is 4 V. This 4 V appears across both branches, so the current in the 6 ohm resistor is 4 divided by 6, which is 0.67 A, and in the 3 ohm resistor it is 4 divided by 3, which is 1.33 A. As a check the two branch currents add to 2 A, the total, and the larger current flows in the smaller resistance, as expected.

items.stem: Match each quantity in Column I with its SI unit in Column II. Column I: (a) current, (b) potential difference, (c) resistance, (d) electric power. Column II: (i) ohm, (ii) watt, (iii) ampere, (iv) volt.
items.answer: (a) current - (iii) ampere. (b) potential difference - (iv) volt. (c) resistance - (i) ohm. (d) electric power - (ii) watt.

items.stem: Match each material in Column I with its typical use in Column II. Column I: (a) copper, (b) nichrome, (c) tungsten, (d) rubber. Column II: (i) lamp filament, (ii) insulation on wires, (iii) connecting wires, (iv) heating element.
items.answer: (a) copper - (iii) connecting wires, for its very low resistivity. (b) nichrome - (iv) heating element, for high resistivity and resistance to oxidation. (c) tungsten - (i) lamp filament, for high resistance and a very high melting point. (d) rubber - (ii) insulation on wires, being a non-conductor.

items.stem: Draw a labelled circuit diagram to verify Ohm's law, and state what you would measure and plot.
items.answer: Draw a battery of several cells in series, using the long-and-short-line symbol for each cell, and label it battery. From its positive terminal draw a line to a plug key, shown as a break with a lever, and label it key. Continue to a rheostat, drawn as a rectangle with an arrow across it, and label it rheostat for varying the current. Continue to an ammeter, drawn as a circle containing A, and label it ammeter in series. Continue to the resistance wire under test, drawn as a plain rectangle and labelled R. Complete the loop back to the negative terminal of the battery. Now draw a voltmeter, a circle containing V, connected across the two ends of R only, and label it voltmeter in parallel with R. Mark solid dots at every junction. Annotate the diagram with the procedure: close the key, adjust the rheostat to obtain a small current, record the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V, then repeat for five or six different settings of the rheostat. Annotate what to plot: V on the vertical axis against I on the horizontal axis. Annotate the expected result: a straight line through the origin, whose slope gives the resistance R, confirming that V is proportional to I. Add two cautions: the key should be opened between readings so the wire does not heat and change its resistance, and the ammeter must be in series while the voltmeter must be in parallel, since reversing them would short the circuit.

items.stem: Draw circuit diagrams of three resistors in series and the same three in parallel, and annotate each with how current and voltage behave.
items.answer: Draw the first diagram with a battery, a key and three rectangles labelled R1, R2 and R3 joined end to end in a single loop, with an ammeter in the loop. Annotate it: there is only one path, so the same current I flows through every resistor; mark the ammeter reading as I at more than one point in the loop to make this explicit. Draw three voltmeters, one across each resistor, and label their readings V1, V2 and V3, annotating that V1 plus V2 plus V3 equals the supply voltage V, and that the largest share falls across the largest resistance. Write beside the diagram Rs equals R1 plus R2 plus R3, and note that the total exceeds the largest individual resistance. Add a warning annotation: a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. Draw the second diagram with the same battery and key, and the three resistors each connected between the same pair of junction points, marked with solid dots, so that all three lie side by side. Place one ammeter in the main line before the junction and one in each branch. Annotate it: the same potential difference V appears across every branch, so draw a single voltmeter across the pair of junctions. Label the branch currents I1, I2 and I3 and annotate that they add to the total I, and that the largest current flows through the smallest resistance. Write beside the diagram one over Rp equals one over R1 plus one over R2 plus one over R3, and note that the total is less than the smallest branch. Add the annotation that each branch can be switched independently and a break in one leaves the others working, which is why houses are wired this way.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to verify Ohm's law and explain how the results establish it.
items.answer: Set up a circuit containing a battery of several cells, a plug key, a rheostat, an ammeter in series and the resistance wire under test, with a voltmeter connected in parallel across that wire alone. The ammeter must be in series so that it carries the current being measured, and the voltmeter in parallel so that it reads the potential difference across the wire; the ammeter is chosen with very low resistance and the voltmeter with very high resistance so that neither appreciably disturbs the circuit. Close the key, adjust the rheostat so that a small current flows, and record the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V. Open the key. Repeat for five or six progressively larger currents, opening the key between readings so that the wire does not warm up. Now examine the results in two ways. First, compute the ratio V divided by I for each pair of readings. The values are found to be equal within the accuracy of the instruments, and that constant ratio is the resistance of the wire. Second, plot V on the vertical axis against I on the horizontal axis. The points lie on a straight line passing through the origin, and the slope of that line equals the same constant. Both treatments establish the same conclusion: V is directly proportional to I, which is Ohm's law, and the constant of proportionality is the resistance. Three features of the method are essential to the proof. Several readings are needed, since a single pair would determine a ratio but could not establish proportionality. The line must pass through the origin, since a straight line not through the origin would show a linear relation but not a proportional one. And the key must be opened between readings, because the resistance of a metal rises with temperature; if the wire is allowed to heat, the later points fall off the line and the law appears to fail when in fact its stated condition of constant temperature has been violated. That last point is worth keeping, since it shows the experiment can also demonstrate the limits of the law: repeating it with a filament lamp instead of a wire gives a curve rather than a line, because the filament heats greatly and its resistance is not constant.
